subject: chemistry
title: Required practical: acid-alkali titration
key_idea: A titration finds the volumes of an acid and an alkali that react exactly. A pipette measures a fixed volume of one solution into a flask with an indicator. A burette adds the other until the colour changes. Repeat until results agree.

blocks.text: This section covers what each piece of apparatus does and which indicators to use. The acids used are hydrochloric, sulfuric or nitric acid, with an alkali such as sodium hydroxide.

items.meaning: A method that finds the volumes of an acid and an alkali that react exactly with each other.
The point at which the indicator just changes colour and the solution is neutralised.
Repeat titres that agree closely, within 0.10 cm³ of each other.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others.

items: **Pipette:** measures a fixed volume accurately, such as 25.0 cm³. Use a pipette filler.
**Burette:** measures variable volumes. It can add a solution drop by drop and is more accurate than a measuring cylinder.
**Conical flask:** holds the solution being titrated. Stand it on a white tile to see the colour change.
**Indicator:** a few drops show the end-point.

blocks.text: Do not use universal indicator. It changes colour gradually, so it does not show a sharp end-point.

items: A pipette measures a fixed volume. A burette measures variable volumes.
Use a single indicator such as methyl orange or phenolphthalein, not universal indicator.

blocks.text: Here the alkali is in the flask and the acid is in the burette. It works the other way round too.

diagram.alt: Put the steps of a titration in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the titration method in order
steps: Rinse the burette with the acid and the pipette with the alkali
Use a pipette and filler to put 25.0 cm³ of alkali into a conical flask
Add a few drops of indicator and stand the flask on a white tile
Fill the burette with acid and record the initial reading
Add acid from the burette, swirling the flask
Add the acid drop by drop near the end-point, until the indicator just changes colour
Repeat until you have concordant results

items: The first titration is a rough titration. It finds the approximate end-point quickly.
In the accurate titrations, add the acid slowly near the end-point, drop by drop.
Read the burette at eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus, with no bubbles in it.
To make a pure, dry salt, mix the same volumes again without the indicator, then evaporate and crystallise.
Pipette in the alkali, add indicator, then add acid from the burette until the colour changes.
Do a rough titration first, then repeat accurately until the results agree.

blocks.text: Careful technique and repeats give an accurate titre. The titre is the volume of acid added from the burette.

items: Swirl the flask while adding the acid, to mix the reactants.
Use a white tile to see the end-point more clearly.
Add slowly near the end-point, so you do not overshoot.
Rinse the burette with the acid first. Water would dilute the acid and give an inaccurate result.
Repeat the titration and take a mean of the concordant results.

blocks.text: Leave out the rough titration and any anomalous result when calculating the mean.

blocks.label: Mean titre
blocks.formula: mean titre = (titre 1 + titre 2 + ...) ÷ number of titres used
where: use only the accurate, concordant titres

diagram.alt: Calculate the mean titre from two accurate titrations, leaving out the rough titration.
diagram.question: A rough titration needed {r} cm³ of acid. Two accurate titrations needed {a} cm³ and {b} cm³. Calculate the mean titre using the accurate titrations only.
working: Leave out the rough titre of {r} cm³.
Divide by 2 to get the mean: {answer}

items: Swirl, use a white tile and add drop by drop near the end-point.
The mean uses only the accurate, concordant titres.

checks.q: Give two reasons why a burette is used to add the acid.
checks.a: Any two from: it can add the acid in small increments (drop by drop), it can measure variable volumes, it is more accurate than a measuring cylinder.

checks.q: Name an indicator for a titration and give its colour change when acid is added to the alkali in the flask.
checks.a: Methyl orange, from yellow to red (or orange). Or phenolphthalein, from pink to colourless.

checks.q: A titration gives titres of 24.80, 24.45, 24.50 and 24.55 cm³. The first is anomalous. Calculate the mean titre.

exam_phrases: add the (sulfuric) acid (from the burette) until the colour (of the indicator) changes
use a (volumetric) pipette to add the alkali into a conical flask
add (a few drops of) indicator (to the alkali)
read the volume from the burette / take the initial burette reading
swirl; use a white tile; add the acid dropwise (near the end-point); repeat and calculate a mean
pipette measures a fixed volume (accurately), burette measures variable volume
methyl orange from yellow to red / orange / pink; phenolphthalein from pink to colourless

mistakes.wrong: Add universal indicator to the alkali in the flask.
mistakes.right: Universal indicator is not accepted. Name a single indicator: methyl orange, phenolphthalein or litmus.

mistakes.wrong: The mean of 8.95, 9.00, 8.85 and 8.45 cm³ is 8.81 cm³.
mistakes.right: The anomalous result must not be included. Use 8.95, 9.00 and 8.85 only: 26.80 ÷ 3 = 8.93 cm³ to 3 significant figures.

mistakes.wrong: A pipette and a burette both measure variable volumes.
mistakes.right: A pipette measures a fixed volume accurately. A burette measures variable volumes and can add the solution drop by drop.

worked_example.question:
This is part of the method the student used for the titration.

1. Measure 25.0 cm3 of the sodium hydroxide solution into a conical flask using a pipette.
2. Add a few drops of indicator to the flask.
3. Fill a burette with citric acid solution.

Describe how the student would complete the titration.
answer_points: Add the citric acid (to the flask) until there is a permanent colour change.
Measure or record the volume of citric acid added, by taking the final and initial burette readings.
Any one from: swirl; use a white tile; add the acid dropwise or slowly near the end-point; repeat and calculate a mean.
worked_example.tip: One mark each. The colours of the indicator are not needed.

blocks.text: (Separate science) Titration is assessed in the GCSE Chemistry course only, not in the combined science course.
(Higher tier) You may also be asked for calculations of concentration in mol/dm³ and g/dm³ from titration results. This note covers the practical technique only.

exam_phrases: read the (initial) volume on the burette
open the tap / add acid to {alkali / flask}
swirl the mixture until end point / until indicator changes colour
(close tap then) read (final) volume of acid in burette
use of white tile, easier to see precisely when indicator changes colour
(near to end point) {add (acid) slowly / in small quantities each time}
use a pipette filler; draw the liquid up so the bottom of the meniscus touches the line
rinse burette with acid, because water would dilute the original acid

mistakes.wrong: The burette is rinsed with acid to avoid contamination.
mistakes.right: 'To avoid contamination' is ignored. Water in the burette would dilute the acid and give an inaccurate result.

mistakes.wrong: Stir the flask during the titration to get an accurate titre.
mistakes.right: 'Stir' is ignored. Say swirl the flask, and add the acid slowly or in small amounts near the end point.

mistakes.wrong: The mean of 27.65, 24.70, 24.80 and 24.60 cm³ is 25.44 cm³.
mistakes.right: Leave out the rough titration. The accurate titrations give (24.70 + 24.80 + 24.60) ÷ 3 = 24.70 cm³.

mistakes.wrong: Water left in the conical flask after rinsing makes the alkali more dilute, so less acid is needed.
mistakes.right: Water in the conical flask does not change the amount of alkali, so there is no effect. Water in the pipette does dilute the alkali and decreases the titre.

worked_example.question:
The volume of dilute sulfuric acid required to neutralise 25.0 cm3 of ammonia solution can be found by titration.

In the titration, a few drops of methyl orange indicator were added to the ammonia solution in a conical flask before adding the dilute sulfuric acid.

The titration was repeated to obtain a mean volume of dilute sulfuric acid required to neutralise the 25.0 cm3 of ammonia solution.

The volumes of the two solutions were measured accurately.

Explain two other practical steps that should be used in the titration to ensure that an accurate titre volume is obtained.
answer_points: Use a white tile, because it is easier to see precisely when the indicator changes colour.
Near the end point add the acid slowly, in small quantities each time, so it is easier to stop before excess acid is added.
Alternatively, swirl the flask when adding the acid, to ensure complete mixing of both reactants.
Alternatively, rinse the burette with acid, the pipette with ammonia and the flask with water beforehand, so there are no impurities to affect the result.
worked_example.tip: Choose two steps. Each needs its reason to score both marks.

exam_phrases: add indicator, e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange or litmus, to the acid in the conical flask
swirl the conical flask (after adding the sodium hydroxide)
dropwise addition at the end point / until the indicator just changes colour
phenolphthalein: colourless to pink; methyl orange: red to yellow
use a single indicator rather than a mixed indicator, to give a sharp endpoint
use a white tile under the conical flask to see the endpoint more clearly
the mean is calculated using the concordant values / values within 0.10 cm³

mistakes.wrong: Add a few drops of universal indicator and stir the flask.
mistakes.right: Universal indicator is not allowed for a titration. Swirl, shake or mix is allowed, but stir is ignored.

mistakes.wrong: Titration 1 (24.80 cm³) is not included in the mean because it is the rough titration.
mistakes.right: 'It is a rough titration' is ignored. Titration 1 is left out because it is anomalous: it is not concordant with the others.

mistakes.wrong: To improve the experiment, repeat the titration.
mistakes.right: 'Repeat the titration' is ignored. Give a specific improvement with its reason, for example adding the alkali dropwise near the end point so the indicator changes on one drop.

worked_example.question:
Student A does a titration with an acid and an alkali.
He uses dilute sulfuric acid, sodium hydroxide solution and an indicator solution.
The student adds sodium hydroxide solution from the burette to the sulfuric acid until the indicator changes colour.
He then adds a few more drops of sodium hydroxide to be certain the sulfuric acid is neutralised.
He takes the final volume reading on the burette to find out how much acid reacts with 25.0 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution.

Describe and explain how the student could improve his experiment to get a more accurate value.
answer_points: Do not add more sodium hydroxide after the indicator changes colour, because the indicator changes colour at the end-point and extra alkali makes the solution alkaline.
Add the sodium hydroxide dropwise or slowly towards the end-point, because the indicator should change colour on one drop.
Use a single indicator rather than a mixed indicator such as universal indicator, because a single indicator gives a sharp end-point.
Swirl the flask during the addition, to mix the acid and alkali. Or use a white tile, to see the end-point more clearly.
worked_example.tip: Any four points score. Each improvement is paired with its reason.
